entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: March 19, 1991 Interview

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: The following interview was conducted by Bob Zybach at the home of Velma Carter Rawie in Corvallis, Oregon.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: 1. Family Photographs

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I'm Velma Rwie and my parents were Elmer Pearl Carter, and Rose Elizabeth Carter. I am the great granddaughter of Tolbert and Martha Angeline Carter, who were. . . came out in 1845 I believe it was and settled on a Donation Land Claim in the Palestine. . . The area that is called Palestine where the old Palestine cemetery and church is.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: The first question I'd like to ask is did any stories of the Oregon Trail, crossing the Oregon Trail, come through your family?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: The closest thing that I have to crossing the Oregon Trail was in a report made by my great grandfather at one of the conventions for the Oregon Pioneers Association and he gave a report of some of the trials and tribulations they had crossing the plains.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: You have a copy there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I have a copy of it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. Would you mind jf we made of copy of that and maybe put it as an appendix to this interview? [See Appendix B]

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I would be happy for you to do that, and as I say, I have two other copies of this so I would like to have this one back but, it's not quite as important that I get it back.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: 1 guarantee that you will get it back.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: But it tells a lot about the family and arriving in this part of the country. The Applegate Trail and whatnot; a lot of it. It's really interesting reading.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. Do you know the history of your family before they came to the states?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I really don't.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: This is the earliest that you know?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes. My mother especially, because my father died at fifty seven, he was very

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: young when he died, and my mother was. . . she didn't like the old fashioned stuff. Well she just didn't have any antique furniture or anything because when the modem waterfall furniture caine out that was what she wanted. Even at ninety three she was a very modern person. By modern I don't mean wild and woolly, she liked new things.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was it your grandma that lived to be 102?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: My great grandmother.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Great grandmother.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Great grandmother that lived to be 102.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Would she be the wife of...

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: She was the wife of Tolbert Carter and her name was Martha Angeline.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Can you remember Tolbert?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't remember Tolbert. He died... Oh, but the biggest thrifi was to go to my great grandmother's on Sunday afternoon. Of course we didn't get to go to the parlor very often. But we always basically lived.. . in the kitchen

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Why didn't you go in the parlor?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, you know in those days parlors weren't for the kids to play in. That was where the nice ladies were. Their home was out by Palestine church and cemetery.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What do you remember about her?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, the thing that always . . . that 1 am amused about is in those days we had rural telephones, you know, the crank telephones on the wall, and her easy chair was right by the telephone. It didn't make any difference whose ring came on the telephone, Grandma picked up the receiver and if she didn't get it she'd say, "What's that you say?"

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [Laughter]

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Everybody expected her. They knew Grandma Carter was on the line, on anybody's phone, but they just took it for granted. After all, at a 103 I guess you could listen if you wanted to.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So everybody was...

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Everybody was. . . they might not have liked it but nobody objected to it.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [Laughter]

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: It's pretty hard to get mad at a 103 year old lady.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, uh huh. And she was really active up until her death you might say. She packed her water from the spring, she didn't have hot and cold water and one of her sons, Perry [Carter], lived right next door to her home. And uh... as I say, she was slightly built and she got more slightly built as time went on. People had the tendency to. . . they get a little more stooped although she wasn't really a stooped person.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Uh huh.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: But she was.. . I wish I had some pictures but then you wouldn't be interested..

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, I'm definitely interested in pictures!

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I will have to get.. . I fixed up a scrap book of pictures for both of my sons... of the old pictures of my great grandma.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: U/i huh. I'd be vely interested...

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Is that [recorder] on? I'm gonna go get it. [Retrieves scrapbook]

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Would it be possible for me to make copies of these?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. You can see that I am pretty slow about returning pictures, but I return them in good shape.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I do have extras, but I don't. . . I just got these not to long ago and I haven't put them in my kids scrapbooks yet, but you could take them.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [Looking at family photos] Now what was her maiden name?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Bileui. B-.i-l-e-u-i. Let me check it to make sure. Martha Bileui.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now did she come out in 1845 also?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Uh huh.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: On the same train?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Mr. [Tolbert] Carter was born in Missouri, November 6, 1825, of English ancestry. In early life he moved to Illinois and started from Morgan county in that state to Oregon in March of 1846. He was married to Mrs. Martha Angeline Bileui on August 13, 1852. So they were married.. . apparently her family was coming across on the piRins at the same time.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: iL/h huh.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't know that, but they weren't married until '52 which would be six years later. But then of course they didn't come out over night like we did too. They could have gotten married along the way someplace.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now, her fanily, did they settle in this area also?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I have no recollection of ever knowing any of Grandma's family.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So would you suppose...

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: And if there were any.. . I don't remember any Bileuis. I'm sony but I am just at a loss there. I just have no idea.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Would your kids ever talk with her? Would she tell you stories of the old days?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Urn. Not more than what I heard from my own grandparents. I was more interested when I went to her house to see her pretty pieces of cut glass and that sort of things. I have the chair that crossed the plains. . . I have some of her cut glass from what I call "Horn of plenty" and it hung on the parlor wall with two blue satin ribbons and whatnot. And I have that glass.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Would it be like a cornucopia?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Like a cornucopia, but it was cut glass.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How many children did they have?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Tolbert... [inaudible] my grandpa, Johnny Carter. . . Perry, uncle Virgil.. [another son of Tolbert's, Elvin Carter, moved to Washington state & never lived around here. VCR]. Mary married a Hodges . . .Clara married a Taylor. . . I think that that would be it [inaudible].

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Would that be the Locke Cemeteiy?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, out at the Palestine Cemetery.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, at the Palestine Cemeteiy.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, none of my family is buried out here at the Locke Cemetery. We were farther north. We were really out in the country.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now that brings up the question was the main town other than Wells. . . if you went to town would it be like to Salem or to...

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Albany. Albany or Corvallis, but Albany was more of a farmer's town. We very seldom came to Corvallis. We went to Albany every Saturday to buy our

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: groceries, but it was only. . . it was rare, I don't remember coming to Corvallis as a kid like I did going to Albany. And mother would go and do the grocery shopping and whatnot and my dad loved automobiles. Whenever a new car came out he had one and he spent time going to dealers in Albany, you know, I mean they weren't like dealers today, to look at the cars and to B.S., so to speak, to the car salesmen. They all knew him and things weren't like they are now when I was growing up. I mean everyone knew everybody pretty much. And then my grandfather, Johnny Carter, had just three children and that was... This is my grandfather, Johnny, and his wife Mary and this was my father and my uncle who's. . . His name is Eston Avery Carter but he was "Mox," uncle Mox. M-o-x.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: He's the one who lived by Coffin Butte?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Uh huh.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: And this is my aunt who married a Tomlinson.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And that is your father?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That is my father.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: JThat is his name?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Elmer Pearl.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Elmer PearL And where did he get the name Pearl?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't know, but I've got it to. I'm Velma Pearl.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Ak Would that be from her family?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't know of any other Pearls that I've never heard in our family except for dad and me.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Viz huk

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: He never went by Elmer. He always went by Pearl or E.P. Carter. He was E.P., all his signatures. . . he never signed any other. . . and he had beautiful handwriting.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I've heard people refer to Pearl Carter so...?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: He was Pearl Carter.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now this is your...?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: This is my grandmother.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What was her name?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Her name was Mary Williamson.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So she was a Williamson?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: She was a Williamson.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you recall who her parents were?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes. They were just Grandma and Grandpa Williamson.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, so they were still alive when you were young.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh yeah. Uh huh, and she had lots of brothers and sisters. They lived more down in the Rickreall - Salem area.In fact, Grandma.. . in her family         she was married, my grandpa and her were married early, I mean while she was quite young.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How old was she then?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: About 15 or 16 and she.., when her family had a family portrait taken one time, my granddad was in that same family portrait.In fact, I have the picture of that if you want to turn that off for a minute.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. [Turned off recorder]

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: . .   dresser in the bedroom back there that I have nothing but old family portraits. This is my grandma and grandpa.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Williamson?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Williamson. Great Grandma and Grandpa Williamson.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now they crossed the Oregon Trail too?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, apparently they did, but I don't know anything about the route they took or anything like that. But this is my grandmother and this is Grandpa [Carter].

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So he got in on the Williamson family portrait?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: But this is the Williamson family portrait.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Ah ha. [Laughter] He's like one of the family maybe?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well I think so. As I say she was quite young, and I think they might have.. . I don't know for sure but I think that they might have lived with Grandma, Great Grandma and Grandpa, for awhile after they were married.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: If they lived in Rickreal4 do you recall any of the family names there? Like say Nathaniel Ford? Did they ever mention the Ford family?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I'm not sure that Grandma and Grandpa, Great Grandma and Grandpa... but I have an uncle Jesse. Let's see, this is Uncle Jesse Williamson. He lived in Rickreall. In fact, I think that their son still lives in Rickreall and his name is Arms, Roscoe Arms. This is Aunt Lizzy. They lived in Salem and her husband's name was Edgar. [Inaudible] This was grandmother's youngest brother and he was a handsome gentleman. Even as he got older he had lots of curly hair. Isn't that funny how I never thought about that but I can remember when Uncle Gussy come to visit. We kids all looked at him like he must be really someone special because he was always dressed nice and stuff. This is beside the point of interest, but that's my mother and myself.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, this is a nice picture of...

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: This is me here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: You're the baby in the picture?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. And my parents were this girl's guardian and raised her. They had her four years before I was born. My mother's half-brother was a blind person and his wife died when she - I call her my sister because we were brought up as sisters - was born. And since Uncle George was blind he couldn't take care of her so my mother and dad were appointed her guardian and raised her and they had never had any children which happens many times After they had had her for four years I came along.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh. Were you the only child?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: And I'm the only child basically, but Bess and I were brought up as sisters.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: You sure were a pretty baby.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh well, my mother did all the sewing of course. These are all mother's sewing made all these clothes for Bess and I. And my sister lives in Vancouver, Washington. We were brought up as sisters although she always went by her dad's name, Bessie Price, but my parents were her Mom and Dad. She called them mom and dad.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was your mother then a Price?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: My mother was a Price from out in the Kings Valley area. You've probably heard the Price name from out in that area.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah. Price Perkin. Do you know her parents names? Your grandparents Price?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Now let me think a minute. You better turn that off a minute [inaudible]. I'm related to an awful lot of people in Benton county. Of course, both of my parents were from Benton county or Polk county, which joins. On mother's birth certificate it just says Polk county. It doesn't say Kings Valley or anything it just says Polk county.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So she was born in Kings Valley?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. Uh huh

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: You mentioned her cousin Anson Price who lives on Maxfield Creek Road. If you went to visit him from Wells, how did you go there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, I don't remember ever going out to visit them when I was a kid. I go to see them now because they're about all the family that is left along that side of the family. The Prices. . . Earl Price died not too many years ago and his mother Rovia Price, .. . You see, there were Anson and Anson's parents (Fred Price) and George, which would be Bess's dad. Great Grandpa Price had those three children and then his wife died and then Grandpa married my grandmother. So my mother and her. . . She had three sisters, four brothers by the second. . . I mean Grandpa Price did by my grandmother. So that was another family. Then my grandmother, after Grandpa Price died, remarried again and moved over to the Lebanon area1.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was he still alive when you were young?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Grandpa Price?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So that part of the family moved to Lebanon?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes. Uh huh. I never. . . I don't remember that part of the Price family until after I was grown basically.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So you were mostly growing up around Carters and Williamsons...?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Williamsons and Hodges. See, those Donation Land Claims were all taken out together, Hodges and up in the Palestine area.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: The Hodges that you were related to, was that Maiy... ?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That was Mary Carter who married a Hodges. Yeah. H-o-d-g-e-s. And they lived down on what we called River Road, which would be Spring Hill Road. Like from Albany. . . the one out Spring Hill Road.. . . out past the golf coarse and you come in Palestine out that way or by Camp Adair coming in from the east to Camp Adair . . . out where the incinerator used to be. That was Spring Hill Road or River Road. . . When we went to Albany, sometimes we'd go River Road just for something different when I was a kid.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So when you were little you always traveled by new car?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, we always had... We had quite a few new cars, but I remember the old Model rs. We had those too though and what we called Ryal's Hill. . . I can remember a lot of times when we had to get out because they were muddy, dirt roads.. . ruts you know, If it was raining really hard, we'd all have to get out and dad would get a running shot at the hifi to make it and now it's no hill at all, but in those days it was a big hill.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What hill Ls Ryal's Hill?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, if you went out to Palestine, you know where the Palestine church and cemetery is. . . Do you from Camp Adair?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: If you go out here, like from here out to what we called the Granger road, you know where the.. . is it still there . . . where the Northwest Natural Gas have tanks out there. You know where that road is?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: And you go north. Ryal's Hill would be the first hill that you, basically the first big hill that you come to. [Laughter] But as I say, in those days it was a big hill.

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: In addition to "Whistling Coon" (the song given for the Month of May on page 13, copyrighted and for sale by Win. A Pond & Co.), a surprising number of songs were printed in the Songster that would be considered degrading to African Americans by today's standards.     These included "Dar's A New Moon in de Sky!" (February's song), "Jericho" (page 11), and the selection for September, "Haul the Woodpile Down." Although the Songeter may not have actually had the."millions of friends and patrons" claimed in its annual message to its readers, it undoubtably had a significant influence on the readers (and singers) of Wells and other rural Oregon communities. Many of these towns, including those along the railroad lines, never had black residents or visitors. The timing of this widespread advertising brochure was only 30 years after the publication of "Uncle Tom's Cabin" and over 50 years before the Hollywood stardom of Stepin Fetchit. The comical and paternalistic depiction of black people in the popular music of the time was probably viewed as positive and supportive, if at all.   The fact that "black music" was nearly 1/3 of the total "new listings" put out by a major throat "gargling oil" manufacturer is of historical interest.

In fact, I have a two-and-a-half dollar gold piece that was his watch fob that I wear as a necklace now that was paid way back when they had box socials and basket socials for entertainment. . . When the ladies fixed up the boxes and baskets and whatnot and the men bid on them and my dad was always the cashier for these things. And this one fella wanted this particular girl's basket awfully bad, of course this was before my time, but this is the way the story goes, and he bid two dollars and a half. In those days, which was a lot of money, and he paid for it with a two-and-a-half dollar gold piece. My dad had the money, so he kept the two-and-a-half dollar gold piece and put the money in. So that was what he wore. Of course, I have his watch, but I took the fob off of it and put it on a necklace.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So all the domestic chores, Bessie was learning that.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, and as I say, to this day. . . well even after we . . . Then as I say, when Camp Adair took over mothers farm out there, we moved back to town and mother moved to town and we both bought new houses in town [Corvallis]. Mother bought one down on Western Avenue. It's where the campus police office is now right across from Parker Stadium. That was the house that she bought and lived in.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, so your mother lived right in the house?

entries.speaker: A

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: This is kind of skipping ahead a little bit but, when Camp Adair got built, it looks like in the aerial photos that there is a lazge expansion of housing in Con'allis. Did a lot of the people from Camp Adair, working constrnction or living there, live in town here?

entries.speaker: caption
entries.text: A Wells-area farmer stops by the Carter Store on his way to the Fisher's Warehouse with a load of grain, c.1900. Local farmers would often stop by the store for a soda or a drink of water and a chance to pick up their mail or "catch up on the gossip."

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: They begged for places for people to live, even after the troops moved out here. Lots of times their families would come out here and they just went from door to door asking for places to sleep . . . other families to sleep. And that's where my youngest son, who was just 50 on Saint Patrick's Day, we call him "Moe", his name is Melvin, but a little gal from Arkansas, who's husband was stationed out here, rented a room from us. We had a big new house and we had lots of room. They don't pronounce their L's or something and she tried to call him "Mel" and it came out "Moe." He's been "Moe" ever since.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did most the families in town... were they cooperative in providing housing?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh yeah, an awful lot of people opened up their homes to them.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was that for patriotism or for income?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Both. It was.. . The people were desperate. Their fRmilies would follow them out here and there was no. . . We weren't prepared. Corvallis or Albany, nobody was prepared for anything like that.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: When the fa,niies had to move from Adair and the government came in and bought the...

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Wait a minute, the government came in before they ever bought it. It was condenination is what it was. But they came in and tore down fences on my mothers farm and started building a railroad spur and all mother knew was that the government was going to take her farm. So, she took her shotgun out and stopped them and she stopped them! She got her money.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now, was your dad...

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: My father was deceased. She was all alone at that time

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So the government came out and were building a raifroad and she attacked them with a shotgun?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, I wouldn't say that she attacked them, but she let them know that it was her property and they were trespassing.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Uh huh. And they stopped?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: And they stopped.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: When the government came out then, that was before Pearl Harbor wasn't it?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, it was after Pearl Harbor. Well now wait, Pearl Harbor was December 7, 1941. Wasn't it?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I think so.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, it all happened all about the same time. Let's face it, they had to have a camp or a place on the west coast. Things grew real fast and mother got, we had a hundred acres, and mother got 100 dollars an acre.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was she upset about that?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, yes! If you had lost your husband and then you lost your home, all within a very short period of time, wouldn't you be upset? You know, I mean that was the only life that my mother knew.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: U/i huh. So how long had your father been dead at that time?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: He died in '37.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And then the government bought [her farm] in '41.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It was '41 because Melvin was born in March of '41 and that was.. . He was just a tiny baby when we moved to town.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Uh huh. And so you were living on the farm with your mother at the time?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Uh huh. Both of my boys were born up there after my father had died.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What was the attitude of the neighbors about the government...

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Terrible! But there was no "ifs", "ands", or "buts".. . just when. An awful lot of the people died very shortly afterwards. When you displace somebody who's been a farmer all of their life basically, they are a little too old to start farming all over again. We didn't have time to go out and buy a farm.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: U/i huh. And a lot of those families had been there for...

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Always.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: their whole lives?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, that was their homes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was there settlement? Did anybody notice that these people started dying?. . .thinking that the displacement was causing that or is that just something that you are thinking back on?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I'm just think back on it now. The people who, within a couple of years . . . I can think of three of four of the men especially... I think it's a little easier for a woman maybe. But a man who doesn't know anything but farming, to move to town.. . and a lot of them, they weren't old people, but.. . and they didn't get enough for their farms to go out and live and buy another farm.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did they remain bitter? They were upset about moving but did they think there was maybe something... they were helping out the war? ... they had to do it, it was their duty?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I can't say how other people felt. My mother was bitter about it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And she stayed bitter?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, no. She wasn't one to carry a grudge but at the time she was... If somebody just came in and said, "We're going to take over your farm and build and army camp, and you've got to get out and you've got to get out now." She had her animals she had to get rid of. She had to find a place to live. It wasn't just her, it was everybody.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I've heard that they went into a lot of the pioneer cemeteries and actually moved them. Was that...?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: There's one cemetery that is called the Ridder's cemetery out on the road that they did fence a small area. It was a private cemetery on the Ridder's ranch. They put a chain link fence around that small area. I can't think of any.. it seems like, no . . . I don't think they actually. . . I don't remember at the time. Of course as I think back, I think, "Why didn't I pay more attention to that?" But at the time when things are happening, you don't think so much about it really. I mean, in the sense of what happened to things because after all, I was fairly newly married and had a young family.    . .   . had problems of my own. Not problems, but responsibilities and stuff. You just don't think. . . but then as I get older and as my grandparents passed away and them my mother, who lived to be 93, now I'm the oldest Carter around. People start asking me questions and I have to really stop and think. I was like a lot of kids when I was growing up, I didn't pay a lot of attention.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: It seemed like there were more important things at the time?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Uh huh.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Then when they came in, they started tearing down the houses and digging up the cemeteries. Did that cause additional problems?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't remember them digging up any cemeteries. I know that they did fence that one. It seems like . . . in the back of my mind there was something about disturbing graves. As I say, I don't for sure...

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about the destiuction of the buildings and fences and... ?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, they just bulldozed those down and tore them up.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: 4. Wells

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did that bother people?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Sure, because when you asked me the question about how many people lived in.. There was an Artisan Hall, that was a Lodge, an Artisan Lodge Hall, that was basically a community meeting place. They had community dances on Saturday night, and they had pie socials and basket socials. That's were it was, on the downstairs part of it. The Christmas plays were always at the Hall because it could seat a lot of people. The whole community would come and it had a stage, you know. You see the train, the passenger train that used to run from Portland to Corvallis, was the Red Electric. It was like a trolley car. It had a overhead electric...

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Electrical line over the... ?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, and there was a thing that went off of the Red Electric that went up and rode the hot wire, so to speak. It was like a street car. . . like used to be in Portland or someplace...

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: A trolley.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: A trolley car. And it was the Red Electric. That was what brought the mail and if it was late, we always used to say that it had jumped the track at Whiteson, which is down around Yamhill someplace. That was the

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Would it actually do that or...?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well it didn't jump the.. . but the rod that went up onto the. . . the electric line that would keep it moving would jump off of the. . . It wasn't that the train actually jumped off of the railroad track, but the trolley [inaudible]. There was a rod that went up like on the old Street cars. I don't know if you remember them.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Just one in Portland.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, well it was the same idea but there was a rod went up from the top. So as I say...

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now was that the only train that came through? The Red Electric? Or did other trains .....

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: The freight trains came through.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: On the same track?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, there were sidings along the way and they'd have to move in to let the mail train go through if a freight train came.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Would the freight run evely day?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: As I recall it did. Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Uh huh. There was a siding there of course because of the grain mill, the flour mill we call it but it was Fisher's mill. They actually didn't do any flour making there but they took the, it was called the elevator I guess

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: A grain elevator?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Grain elevator. But that's where they took in the grain and then it was shipped by train again to the mill in Corvallis where it was processed.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So at the Fisher mill here? So you had a grain elevator, a church, your grandfather's store, the social haiL What was the name of that?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Artisan, that was the name of the Lodge, the Artisan Lodge.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, I see.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: And the Lodge. . . They had the Lodge meetings upstairs once a month or two weeks. . . In the bottom was the dance floor and that's where all the school... all the general elections were held at the Artisan Hall.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Where there any taverns?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, no, no way!

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: No way, huh? Was it a diy community?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well I guess it was. I never even heard about anything to drink as a kid growing up.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was that common in the whole community or just in your family?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I think it was common.. . I'm not saying that nobody probably made any moonshine along the way. I don't know that. But no, no tavern. Just the store. Then there was one. . . I'm trying to think.. . where Mr. Hamen Lewis lived right on the corner and then my grandmother's and grandfather's house and then the store and then Mrs. Noise, who is Tomlinson's grandmother, lived next to that

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: and then there was another house where people by the name of Colemans lived and I don't know if you are familiar with Coleman's Jewelry store downtown. Alfred Coleman was the crippled man who walked on crutches for years. He's dead now. Johnny [Coleman] runs the store now. Alfred Coleman, Johnny's dad, was the son of the Colemans who lived out there. Alfred had polio as a kid, crippled.. . But anyway, they lived there. There was probably. . . And oh, then there was a sub station at Wells to generate electricity for this Red Electric train.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How did it generate electdcity?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't know. I'm not an electrician. I don't know, but it was called a sub station. Some people by the name of Lacey; Lacys, run the sub station. There was a little yellow house there, you know like S.P. . . . S.P., I think about S.P., but their house, the house that the Lacys lived in was sort of a cream colored house and everybody knew that that was the house of the people who ran the sub station. To me it was anyway.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So they were kind of there on a... associated with the business, but other people where more associated with families and community?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, and farming. It was a farming community. But I imagine that there was probably 8 or 10 families who lived in there close. Then in later years, there was a mill that came in, a small sawmill came in, and they shipped lumber out of there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was that Valley Mills?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Valley Mills, yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now, Valley Mills had another mill up in Soap Creek Where those two connected?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I think that that is where they got the logs from. There was a railroad spur, as I say, a siding or whatnot and that's where they loaded the lumber and stuff into the boxcars in Wells. I think the logs where sawed there at Wells. They brought the logs down there and sawed them.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you remember how they brought the logs in?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I'm trying to think.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did the reason the mill locate there because of...

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: because of the railroad.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Where would the lumber go from that point?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well it was shipped all over. I don't know where exactly, but it left there in boxcars.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you remember what kind of lumber they sawed?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, they sawed. . . It was big lumber when I was a kid. I would say, 4x8, I mean it was.. . and it was rough lumber of course. Of course, rough lumber. . . a 2x4 rough lumber is a lot bigger than a 2x4...

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: It wasn't tie rails for the railroad tracks?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, no it was lumber.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you remember the years that that mill was up? About how old you were at that time?

entries.speaker: A

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So the mill would be maybe in the early 30s?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It would be the early 30s.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about the grain elevator?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, it closed. Well the farmers still took there grain there. I think my dad still took his grain there all the time he was farming. Yeah, it did. But he didn't work there anymore.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Would they have a separate operator for the grain elevator or did the fanners... ?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: My dad at one time was the operator there. The farmers, of course, took their grain by horse and wagon and this was before the days of combines of course, it was when the threshing machines went throughout. . . you know. People by the name of Brodie's had the threshing machine and they thrashed for eveiybody in the community and they had their own cook wagon. The biggest thrill for me as a kid was when the cook shack came and I got to eat one meal. . . climb up the ladder and sit on the outside and eat with the harvest crew. We always got to sleep one night in the haystack to keep somebody from stealing the stacks of grain. That was our summer vacation was to get to go out and sleep... [laughter]

entries.speaker: caption
entries.text: This railroad car, and others like it, was used as to bring "Revival Meetings" to Wells and to other communities with railroad service in the late 1800s and early 1900s.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: 5. Farm Life and City Jobs

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Sleep on the haystack one night? What would you do the rest of the time during vacation.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: We didn't have vacations in those days.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So what kinds of activities would you be doing?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Work. In the summer time we picked hops as kids. Mother and Dad always said that he was too heavy a man for such light work as picking hops. He was a veiy slight built person. He just plain didn't want to pick hops, but he pretty much had to be at home. He was a farmer and we had stock to take care of and cows to milk and that sort of stuff. Mother always took Bess and I to pick hops because it was always either too hot or too cold or too wet or too dry. I just hated to pick hops. I remember the first pair of shoes that I ever bought with my own money and I've had thousands of pairs of shoes since that I can't tell you about.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So that hop money was special?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: but I had enough money to buy my own pair of shoes. It's funny I've thought about that a lot because I've always been crazy about shoes as an adult. Out of all of the shoes I've had, I can still see that first pair of shoes that I bought with my own money.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you think that maybe that is why you grew up liking shoes?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [Laughter] I don't know. I don't know, but I always had big feet and I still have big feet. My dad used to say, "But just think how tall you would have been if all of that hadn't turned under for feet!" He always tried to make me feel good about it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Most of the time it was not considered good if you were a tall women.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well I was taller. . . a gangly kid. A tall, gangly kid.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Can you remember, in the hop yards, can you remember any of the Indian workers from the Siletz?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, we never. . . No, I can't.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Can you remember any Indians in the community?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I don't remember any Indians in the community.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about the stories of Indian graveyards or Indian camp sites?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I don't remember any of that at all.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Can you remember anybody finding arrowheads in the fields?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, I have some arrowheads that I have found or that people have found around. In fact I have a couple that we've found since we moved out here to this place in the bottom of the ground.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Just in this house here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, but no, I don't remember anything about Indians.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Any stories of that the old timers. . . so just... How about chinese?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was there a Chinese restaurant in Corvallis or Albany?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't know. I don't know. To be truthful I was a very naive. . . even when I went to Corvallis High school. Because I rode the school bus, I came into town, I got off of the bus, I went to school and when school was out, I got on the bus and went home. It was ten miles and in those days parents didn't run back in forth.. Now don't misunderstand me, I wasn't abused. I had a lot more than most kids did but living in the country you didn't see anything. You didn't go to sports or anything like that.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about movies?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh no. Once in awhile, on a Saturday afternoon, if we went to town we might get to go to a show.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Would you have a radio that you would listen to?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, when the folks got their first radio, I can remember that the farmers from all around them would listen to the prize fights on the radio. That was a big deal for the men especially.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Would that be Jack Dempsey?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, some of the old timers but I can't remember who any of them were. I can remember people coming to listen to the radio because, as I say, Dad always had money for the things. We were very self-sufficient as I say. We separated and sold the cream, we bought groceries and we sold eggs and bought groceries, but we had our own milk to use and we churned our own butter. We fed the skim milk to the pigs. We sold the pigs when they became fat. We cured our own ham and bacon and that sort of stuff.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you have an orchard?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, we had an orchard. We had our own apples and pears and that sort of stuff and a walnut tree as I recall. Most people were just very self-sufficient.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Were people. . . Did they read newspapers much or was there discussion about books?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I can't remember. . . Yeah there was a paper, a daily paper. If there wasn't a newspaper how else would we start a fire. [Laughter] Really, papers were used for starting the fire and in our old farmhouse, we had an old house and then my parents did build a new house . . . We hadn't been in it too awful long when my father died. . . In the old house, we had a great big square kitchen with a wood stove in it and a dining table. It was a living kitchen. The only other heat in the house was a fireplace in the living room. So, we lived basically in the kitchen area.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And then the living room, was that for entertaining guests?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, often times in the evenings I can remember we sat in the kitchen because it was warmer and it had an upstairs and one bedroom downstairs.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What did you do with the house, the old house, after you built the new one?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Tore it down, we tore it down. In fact, we tore it down and built the new house where that old one was and lived in the garage, the old garage. In the old house that we lived in, I can remember the old round tub we took a bath in on Saturday night. We didn't like that idea so we bought a bath tub, an iron bathtub. You know, with the things on it, claw feet legs, and put it in the corner of this kitchen and dad built a board top for it and attached it to the wall and mother padded it with, we call it creton, a pretty print material and made a ruffle all that way around it, you know. Then when on Saturdays we wanted to take a bath, we had a bathtub. That's where . . . When the lid was down it was like a lounge or something. Dad would come in from work and while he was waiting for dinner to get on the table he would lay down on that. You know, down by the wood stove and as I always said if we got caught taking a bath, we could always put the lid down. [Laughter]

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was that kind of a ritual, a Saturday evening bath?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, of coarse Dad always cleaned up more. I mean being a farmer and

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: working outside, but basically.. . Then of course after we got into the new house, we had running water in the bathroom and that sort of stuff. By the time I started High School we had warm water and facilities and whatnot.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now the old house, did that come down through your family?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, my folks bought that farm. . . let's see, I was about a year old when Mom and Dad bought the farm, that particular one.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now, you're descended from Tolbert Carter.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Right.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: But there jg also a Smiley Carter?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That would be . . . I think Smiley. . . I'm not sure whether Smiley or Smiley's dad and my Tolbert Carter were brothers or something. . . . were related or something, but I don't know. There was a Harry Carter too who lived in Wells there and he was a cousin of my grandpas. In fact, it's interesting that you should mention Snilley, just last week I had a letter, it was a letter addressed to my husband, Ralph Rawie, and the letter said, "Someone told me that a Rawie married a Carter, Rose Carter's daughter and I am writing to all of the Rawies that I. . . because I am a descendent of Johannan Carter and I understand that Rose Carter's daughter married a Rawie." But anyway, and I have contacted her since. She was someone from California. She is checking up on her genealogy and she was trying to find out something.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was Johannan Carter one of the Carter family?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, he would be . . . she told me in the second letter that I got from her after I wrote to her... I said that, "I have no knowledge of Johannan Carter, but my great grandfather was Tolbert." And when she wrote back she said, "I think to get to Johannan you have to go one generation beyond.. . before Tolbert." I had no knowledge of anything before that. But then you're talking about Indians. One time I got a letter from somebody in California who wanted to know if I was related to Sitting Bull and it boiled down to, her daughter was trying to adopt an Indian baby and you can't. . . apparently unless you have some Indian blood in you, you can't adopt an Indian child.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: There are rules like that.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Anyway, so this lady was a Carter and she was trying to find out if maybe there might be some Indian blood in her. [Laughter] My husband laughed and he said, "Well if you've got any Indian blood in you I want to know about it. I want some of this free money that the government is always giving out." [Laughter] It was kind of a standing joke, but that is beside the point.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: When you were growing up, you said in the summer one of the things you did was pick hops.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about the rest of the summer?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: There was.. . On a farm we all had to work basically.                         -

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Would you churn butter or gather eggs?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, and feed the chickens and. . . I don't know, there was always something to do. I can't remember ever sitting down.. . we did read the funnies I guess when the paper come. But I can't remember. . . we read library books I guess. Bess loved, my older sister loved to read. There again I was a tomboy. Now, I was outside all of the time.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What did you do for fun?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, we never had a horse to ride. That was a non-profit, a non-producing animal, A riding horse. We had to just ride the old work horses. We had one that was named Clyde and so I'd get a bridle and get on him and he'd take it about so long and then there was a limb on an old apple tree and he'd go under that and knock me off when he had had enough of riding around in the pasture. He was smart.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Would you ever fish?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, never fished until I was married. My husband was a fisherman. There was no place to fish I guess.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Vhat was the nearest creek?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Soap Creek I guess.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So that would be up north by...?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: . Sulphur Springs. Luckiamute river, we went to pick hops down on the Luckiamute, down close to the Luckiamute river.

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: (End of tape 1, side 2)

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: We weren't abused, I'm not trying to say that. We had lots to eat and had a real good life. I'm not trying to say that I was deprived of anything. At times when I got into High school I wished that I could have participated more in things that kids in town did, like going to ball gaines and whatnot. But I couldn't because, I mean. . . now my son and daughter.. . they run all over the country taking their kids to things but in those days...

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: When you came into town, was there any problems with the city kids as opposed to the farm Idds? Was there any differences or.. . ?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, I was never considered one of the "in" kids so I was a pretty good student and I had lots of friends in town. There were a couple of kids through High school that were town kids, but.. . Then when I finished High school, I went up to Portland to what was old Benke Walker Business College, at that time, in Portland. I went up there for six months, of course, to learn shorthand, typing and that sort of stuff. Then I came back and went to work as a bookkeeper. Well, in those days people weren't so specific on their things and a bookkeeper did a little shorthand, you know, you were sort of an all around office person, I think. At least where I worked. I worked one term at the Legislature for one of the Senators, as his secretary, when I first got out of Business College.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Which Senator was that?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Senator Walker [Oregon Senator]. He was Polk - Benton County Senator. He was from down around the Independence area. That was quite an experience for a country girl, to go and do that. Then as I say, I went to work for an attorney in town for awhile. Jim Lane, who was a blind man and that was the only job I ever got fired from because I.. . When he would get ready to go over to the [Benton County] Court House, he smoked chain cigarettes so he always had ashes all around him, and I kept always whisking him and when he was going to go, well you know, I didn't want him going over there looking like that. His wife said, "I don't need you to . .

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Just because you were whisking...?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, she was a very overbearing person and I think that she just liked for him to look a little sloppy.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Huh! What reason do you suppose that was?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, she just said that I wasn't hired to take care of his personal things. I was hired to do secretarial work.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How long did you work for him?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I think a couple of years. Then I went to work for Bede]in, old Medo-Land Creamery. I was a bookkeeper and that is where I was working up until the day that my oldest son was born. Then I never did go back to work permanently. I worked.. . I've worked in an awful lot of jobs. The only thing I have really never done is wait tables. [Laughter]

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: On purpose?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, I just. . . yeah, on purpose I guess. I just could never carry, I wasn't coordinated enough to pack two cups of coffee or line up a bunch of plates. I never tried it. Let's face it, I knew my limitations. I have clerked in different 2kinds of stores; dress shops, drug stores. I think I'm quite a capable person. I can do most anything if I make up my mind. . except wait tables.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [Laughter] Uh huh.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I guess I really never wanted to wait tables or I probably would have.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: 6. Sulphur Springs Picnics

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So it was a blessing. [Laughter] We were talking about going to the Luckiamute sometimes for swimming and one thing that I wanted to do i to look at these pictures of the people at Soap Creelç and I was wondering how often would you go to Soap Creek or Sulphur Springs?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, I would say a couple of times a summer we would have a picnic like this up there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: A couple of times a year.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: But, maybe just on a.. . Have you ever tasted the water up there?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, repeatedly. Eve,ybody that takes me up there makes me drink it. [Laughter]

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Not me.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: You've never even tasted it?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh yes, I've tasted it. A lot of times we'd go up there on Sunday afternoons just

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: to get a drink of water. Just for something to do, the family would go up there. Can you remember any structures up there, picnic tables or a house?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: We must have had some tables. . . No, there was never anything much up there. This is me.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, you're the...

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I'm the tall one of these. And this is the little, the little Torgeson girl that lived.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, that was a year younger than you?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: A year younger than me.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I don't think that we got that on the tape, but they were your neighboring family and then Esten Carter was her aunt and uncle and yours also.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, that's right. This is. . . well now do you remember the Barzee family?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: lived on the way up to Sulphur Springs.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now there are two Barzee families; one by Ed Blakes and one by Tampico.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Airight, this would be one in the same, I would say. This is Arnold and this is Leah and this is Fern Barzee. He was the mail carrier here in Corvallis until he retired several years ago.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So that would be the two little girls?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Uh huh. And that is the boy. I don't know who this is and I haven't found anybody.. . Arnold doesn't know and neither do either one of the girls, who this kid was.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Uh huh. It looks almost like he is wearing kind of a Swiss costume.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: U/i huh. Now can you remember...?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Now this is my Grandfather Carter.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now he is the one in the vest on the left...

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, who has the store.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: facing the camera?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: This is [inaudible] . . . uncle, Jesse, who lived at Rickre all. This is Grandma, my grandma's brother right here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So that is a Williamson?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: So that is a Williamson.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, and who is the man between the two of them?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: And that is a Dodele. That is Gus Dodele and Gus Dodele married a Williamson girl. Gus Dodele's wife was a cousin of my dads.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Uh huh.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: And this. . . yeah, that's Gus. . . This is Paul, I think this is Paul Dodele here. Yeah, Paul Dodele is the one the paid the two-and-a-half dollar gold piece for the box lunch.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So the Dodeles are off to the left there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, this one, this was a Williamson. This is Aunt Ella Williamson and Aunt Ella would be Gus' mother. This is Clyde Tomlinson and that was my Aunt Mattie . . . married this man, Clyde Tomlinson. This is Roy Torgeson he's the father of this little girl here and this is her mother right here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And what was her name?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Nina. Nina Torgeson. This is Uncle Rob Williamson. He's Aunt Ella Williamson's husband. This is my mother and...

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: It is kind of hard to look at this shorter, smaller version here.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, uh huh. And the other girl took the bigger one. And now this was a Holman and the Holmans are related to the Willianisons and the Carters.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Where would the spring be in relation to this...?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It was right about down in here someplace.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, so this is a big opening right in front of the spring?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, and the [Soap] creek ran through here. There was a little creek that ran through here. I'll never forget. . . maybe I've told you this story before. . . one time when we were up there for a picnic, the Woodcocks, who were one of the Corvallis people who had the Woodcock Garage here in Corvallis. One of the Woodcock boys.. . Accidentally, while he was wearing a suit and his good shoes, I remember and he drove his car in the [Soap] creek. I don't know how he got the car, but he got the car stuck in the creek. Not to let on like it was his fault, he got out and started washing it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, so just like...

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Just like it was a perfectly normal thing to do.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: like it was perfectly normal to be stuck in the creek there? Uh huh. How did he get out?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I can't remember that part of the story but I remember hearing my dad say...

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now the Woodcocks, they sold cars didn't they?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What would you do there at the picnics?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, the fellas pitched horseshoes and the ladies stood around and visited. They didn't always pitch horseshoes but they always had some horseshoe pitching. The main thing was to eat. They had the most wonderful food that you ever saw in your life, a potluck type of thing but not everybody took just one thing. They just took food. [Laughter]

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Then shared between... ?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh yeah. It was put out on the picnic table and everybody passed through and took what they wanted and would sit down on the grass or on blankets and whatnot.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Would they have wrestling matches or foot races?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No. Oh sometimes the kids would have a sack race or three-legged race or something like that. I remember horseshoe pitching more than anything else for the men to. . . [inaudible]. And then a lot of them there again, were happy just to have a day off where they could just sort of sit down, visit, and relax.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did anybody swim in the creek or catch fish?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: There wasn't enough water in the creek to swim in. We went wading. Everybody went wading. To swim, no. Now.. . oh, that man is a Douglas there, Harry Douglas. He lived in that house at the north end of Coffin Butte [inaudible] This was one of his daughters, that was a Phelps.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now the whole community would go out there. Would that be because you were all relatives or was that normal for communities to go picnicking?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It just seemed to be a normal thing.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Uh huh.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Maybe it was kind of a family reunion picnic. Basically as you sit and look at this, somebody in this picture is related to everybody in the picture.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Some of them are up from the Luckiamute?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Uh huh. And the Holmans were from Albany basically.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So it was like a local gathering place for families?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, uh huh.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Would there be other people...?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That is my dad right there, he's cut off, but that is my dad right there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Would other families be out there? Would you encounter other people or was it pretty much secluded?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Everybody that was there was our group whether or not there was other people around. . . as I suppose somebody like that Woodcock that I remember. He came out. I think probably other people came to drink the water or something. We would basically go and spend the whole day, I mean this was a big deal.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Would this be for the Fourth of July or just everybody would just say, 'Nat Saturday we're gonna go up to Sulphur Springs?"

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, I guess that is the way it was. It wasn't just on the Fourth of July. I never remember any fireworks as a kid.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Would you go out there for wedding receptions?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, no.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Just for picnics?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: We just went for a picnic. This was a big deal.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you know any of the families out in the Sulphur Springs area?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, the Goviers and you mentioned the Ed Blakes and the Barzees and...

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now the Barzees weren't related to you were they?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, but they were part of the community. As I say, it wasn't all a. . . It wasn't a family reunion, it was a community picnic.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you know the Glenders?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Would you ever visit with any of those families; Glenders or Goviers?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, I saw one of the Glender girls just the other day because one of the

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Glenders married my sister-in-law's brother. That would be on my husband's side. The Glenders had two girls. There were two families of Glenders, brothers married sisters and they lived in the same house and only one of them had children but you never would have known who was the parents to those two girls. I often wondered if the girls knew who, well you know, because they were brought up...

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: The mother and the aunt were both kind of the moms?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, that's right.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did the community think that was odd that brothe,c and sisters were living in the same house and ma,ried like that?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, it was two brothers married two sisters. They always farmed together and they just always lived in the same house. They did that until after the camp came in.. . They went over to Albany, you know where the Swept Wing Motel is in Albany out by the airport, like if you went from Albany heading toward Lebanon on Highway 20 and you cross over the freeway [1-5] there's a restaurant there called the Swept Wing Restaurant on the east side of the freeway. There is a farm out that sits right there and that is where the Glenders moved to when Camp Adair came in.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I talked to Eugene Glender and he said that they moved to Albany but he didn't say where.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: and Art and Leon were still living there after Leon's.. . Elvera is Gene's mom. [Elvera is actually Gene's sister. See Monograph # 9]
bracketed_corrections: [Elvera is actually Gene's sister. See Monograph # 9]

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Would sometimes the Goviers or Glenders go with you to Sulphur Springs?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I can't remember them being out to Sulphur Springs but they probably did. The ladies had a quilting club, they met once a month and. . . quilting quilts .. . a sewing club I guess or something like that. I have a quilt that was made... everybody made a block and they embroidered their name on it. My mother had this quilt and I still have it.. . of all the ladies in the community who went to this quilting club.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Would there be... ?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: And the Glenders, as I said .....they would be there sometimes.

entries.text: 7. Local Families

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: One question I have is, how come Wells and Wellsdale. . . How come the station had a different name than the town?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I can't tell you why except that it was. . . The depot part of it was Wellsdale and the post office was Wells.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you know where the name Wells came from?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you know the Calloways?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, but I've heard my folks talk about the Calloways. I never knew them, but the name rings a bell.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you know a family named Cahoon?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Cahoon?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Cahoon..

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [Inaudible]

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Brown. How about Brown? Did you know any Browns up by...

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: They were farther down, closer to Suver. In [inaudible] there were some Browns down there anyway. [Inaudible]

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Robert McClain?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. That would by Yvonne?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Evonne. She was related to the Browns. See, the McClain's place joined my folk's place.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: The McClains were your next door neighbors?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, to the north. . . and the Ackerrnans, both were north. Their properties joined. Robert, he had a sister, he had several sisters. Doris, his older sister, married George Dannen. The Dannens are not the only ones who still live in that area. They live in the brick house, like when you cut through Camp Adair on the gate and come out of the Independence Road over there. There is a brick house as you turn to your right and head towards Palestine cemetery. On the left of that street there is a very nice, new type brick house.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And that is the Dannens ...?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That is where George and Doris Dannen live.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: You mentioned recalling the Sheppards. I don't have too much information on them.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, the. . . Johnny Sheppard drove school bus when I was a kid going to school. His sister married a Griffin and they lived up Soap Creek close to where one of the Glenders house used to be, you know, on the corner. You go on up that a road a little ways, before you'd get to the Goviers, the Griffins lived in that house. Goldy, Goldy, Goldy Griffin.. . she was John Sheppard's sister.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And John Sheppard was the one who had the house over at the base of Smith HilL Or was it his father?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I would say that it would be his father. I don't remember Johnny's . . . I remember a bunch of the Griffins. I know that Goldy was a Sheppard, sister of a man named John Sheppard. . . John Sheppard was sheriff of Linn County. I don't think about those people. The name makes you start reminiscing about it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Uh huh. That is one reason why I keep bringing them up. [Laughter]

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: The Sheppards . . . oh no, it's a Griffin, but it would still be the Sheppard family. There are still some of the Griffins that live out around Philomath. That would be Golden.. . John Golden. Some of those kids came out around Philomath [inaudible]... John Griffin was in High school when I was and I think that he still. . . He died just recently. I think that when we had our class reunion he was there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So you still have reunions of the people in Wells? That would be High school reunions?

entries.speaker: A

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: A

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: there on the north side of this road cutting through here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Uh huh.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: where a family lives. Their name is Ivers. The boy Ed Ivers and his wife still live there.

entries.speaker: Q
