entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: 8. Farm Life and Wildlife

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How come, now your mother would have had the option of buying that bacic, wouldn't she?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That particular part where.. . if there was work. . . concentrated buildings where my folks were. There are all of those concrete slabs. It wasn't farm land anymore.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, okay. It had just been too developed?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, they had put in roads and foundations for barracks and all that sort of stuff. They moved my folks house, and it was a new house in that area, moved the house the equivalent of a city block into a grove of trees and it was used as an officers club of some kind. It is gone now, but it was. If you go right north from the game farm from where the house is there is a road that crosses this road and heads north. You go right past where my folks house was. The old locust tree is still standing that was in our back yard.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now, that is a question. I'm interested in some of these plants. Now, that locust tree, do you think trees like that or old orchards should be saved?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, I don't know.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Would it bother you if somebody went and cut that down and turned it into firewood?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, it wouldn't bother me because there is no sentimental value left to that out there. . . It isn't the same country as it was before Camp Adair went in.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: They changed it too much?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, it isn't, it just isn't the same.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Are there areas in that neighborhood that are the same, that kind of give you some sentimental attachment to Wells or to your family fann?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I have a sentimental value to it. I've taken both of my granddaughters out there

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: and shown them where we lived when their dad was born and whatnot. I've made up scrap books and albums showing pictures of the old house and of the school and all of that sort of stuff so that they know their heritage, so to speak, or where they are from. As far as being. . . There is a sentimental attachment to it only because it was where I was born I guess. The whole face of it is just so completely changed that it has really destroyed any personal attachment to it other than this is where I lived. I mean, that locust tree was in the back yard. In my own mind, I am attached to things that happened while I lived out there as a child. I can remember being very ill one time with strep throat or something and my dad. . . we didn't have a phone, but he went someplace and called the doctor, old Dr. Anderson, and he came out and my dad had to go out to the highway, this road here, with a team of horses and pick him up out here. Of course, it was a gravel road at that time. [Inaudible] I remember laying on this couch in what was the living room, I told you, with the fireplace in it. I was running a real high fever and he came in and those were the fanciest shoes for a city man...

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [Laughter]

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: well, they were fancy shoes!

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: All this talk about shoes are kind of making me self-conscious about my own. . .[Laughter]

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh no, they are fine! I mean, I didn't see many of the kind of shoes that Dr. Anderson had on and I remember saying to him that, "You've got mud on those beautiful shoes." He said to my mother. . . she says. . . he said, "She's gonna be airight. Her fever is broken now and she's gonna be airight." He stayed with us for quite a long time that night.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Where was Doc Anderson from?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Here in Corvallis. He had delivered me as a baby.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, so he was your family doctor?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: He was the family doctor.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did he take that as a sign that you were gonna be airight...?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, that fact that I acknowledged the fact that he had dirt on his shoes Well, I had been delirious.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So he was taking that as a sign that you were paying attention...?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I had been running this terrible high fever and when I kind of came to and saw that and made a remark about it he figured that I was gonna be alright.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now, you said that your dad went out with a team of horses, what did he farm with?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Horses.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So he didn't have a tractor?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Heavens no! This was before that days of tractors. People just didn't have tractors.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: But he was modem and had money so did he buy a tractor when tractors came in? Did he purchase a tractor... ?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: He never did have a tractor. He farmed with horses until the day he died.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Till 1937? He had a new car when those came out?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Uh huh. But he had his horses and he had his horse drawn equipment and he plowed. . . and he could plow the straightest furrow you ever saw in your life.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Huh. As you grew up on the farm and you grew up outside and your dad is a real efficient farmer, what kinds of wildlife came into that environment?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: China pheasants.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: China pheasants?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, I can remember Dad having a shotgun and we'd have China pheasant once in awhile.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Would you ever see deer?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't remember ever seeing a deer.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Uh huh. Not the whole time?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, I don't remember. I'm not saying that there maybe wasn't deer there. I don't remember seeing deer.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Can you remember hearing coyotes?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about... We14 you didn't have any water so there were no beaver.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, no beaver. There was no creek.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now, that is part of the fly over though. How about ducks and geese coming over part of your community?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, you'd hear the ducks, [Laughter] the geese, not the ducks, the geese go over,

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: but as I say we weren't close to any creeks or anything so we didn't have any ducks. We raised a few turkeys. We always had chickens and pigs.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Would there be hawks or owls?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh yes, and I was pretty good at shooting them because they'd chase the chickens.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: If you saw a hawk or an owl, it was time to shoot them?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: You'd get them because they would get the chickens.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Would you have a...?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: The first time I ever shot a shotgun, I saw a hawk up in a tree and I took the shotgun and pointed it up like that you know. The gun kicked me and knocked me flat on my back. I can remember that.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Uh huh.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Of course you don't shoot hawks anymore. I guess that they are an endangered species, aren't they?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Urn, I don't think that they are endangered. There are sure a lot of them along I-S.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I bought this place, which is this house here that we lived in here four years before we built this house.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Dixon Creek ran through our property down here and we had racoons and stuff down there. They would come in and get our geese and our chickens. We had.. . a lot of times we had coon hunting. Of course, this doesn't pertain to this area up there when we'd have people come out with their coon dogs and we'd have quite a deal when we'd go out and hunt the coons. Would you do it just for the sport?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It was a sport. Well, and to protect. . . and to try to get rid of the coons, save our chickens and ducks.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So what little wildlife you had out in the Wells areq, pretty much you tried to get rid of?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That's right! Because they were, well they were predators.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about things like moles or field mice?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: We had moles that would bother the gardens and Dad would always shoot them with a shotgun and the concussion would kill them. You had to dig them out right away. We didn't have.. . We had a yard and it was fenced but the yard

entries.text: wasn't the primary, well groomed place that yards are in town. It had a walnut tree and a cherry tree and the big locust tree.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Would you grow flowers?
entries.chapter_ref: 9. The Rawies and the OSC School of Forestry

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh yeah, we always had lots of flowers.
entries.chapter_ref: 9. The Rawies and the OSC School of Forestry

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Your dad didn't figure that that was...?
entries.chapter_ref: 9. The Rawies and the OSC School of Forestry

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That wasn't a farm project. That was mother's project.
entries.chapter_ref: 9. The Rawies and the OSC School of Forestry

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, I see.
entries.chapter_ref: 9. The Rawies and the OSC School of Forestry

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, he worked the garden. I'm not trying to leave the impression that my dad was anti.. . in a joking way he used to say that like, hop picking was too heavy a work for such a light man or too light a work for such a heavy man, whichever way. It was just the opposite of what it was but he always had. . . When we were picking hops, this is going back to the hop picking, he always had dinner ready for us when we got home at night. We had baked potatoes and sliced tomatoes and roasting ears. Now if you can think of a better meal than that. . . and to this day that is my favorite meal.
entries.chapter_ref: 9. The Rawies and the OSC School of Forestry

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Is that right? It reminds you of your dad or just...
entries.chapter_ref: 9. The Rawies and the OSC School of Forestry

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Corn on the cob and baked potatoes and sliced tomatoes. . . and we always had some meat. In those days, when we butchered . . . we had our own smoke house. When we butchered we cured our own ham and bacon and mother canned a lot of meat in those days and the same way with beef. If we killed an animal for beef, we canned a lot of it and she put down the steaks in a brine which were like marinated steaks then.      . .   . delicious beef when she took it out.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Would any of the men ever go on hunting or fishing trips?
entries.chapter_ref: 9. The Rawies and the OSC School of Forestry

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Dad never did. A lot of people did go hunting but Dad never did. He was just.

entries.chapter_ref: 9. The Rawies and the OSC School of Forestry

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: There was a lot of singing. I can remember the singing more than anything else. It wasn't really. . . I guess I have heard about revival meetings or maybe I have seen it on television or something, or should I call it "holy roller". . . I mean they are screaming and hollering you know. That wasn't the type of thing. We called them revival meetings. When this train would come in and this paster would speak and whatnot. Most of the people in the neighborhood came. Maybe we'd have prayer meeting every night for a week or something and then the train would move on.
entries.chapter_ref: 9. The Rawies and the OSC School of Forestry

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Would it just kind a be a "revive your religious interests?"
entries.chapter_ref: 9. The Rawies and the OSC School of Forestry

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, uh huh. As I say, it wasn't any particular religion. I have no idea what religion they were.
entries.chapter_ref: 9. The Rawies and the OSC School of Forestry

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Would there be baptisms?
entries.chapter_ref: 9. The Rawies and the OSC School of Forestry

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, I can remember going to one baptism where we went to the river.
entries.chapter_ref: 9. The Rawies and the OSC School of Forestry

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Would that be the Luckiamute?
entries.chapter_ref: 9. The Rawies and the OSC School of Forestry

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Luckiamute river.
entries.chapter_ref: 9. The Rawies and the OSC School of Forestry

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Would you ever go over to the Willainette?
entries.chapter_ref: 9. The Rawies and the OSC School of Forestry

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I don't ever remember going to the Willamette river for a baptism. I can remember going down to the swimming hole basically.
entries.chapter_ref: 9. The Rawies and the OSC School of Forestry

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What was the swimming hole?
entries.chapter_ref: 9. The Rawies and the OSC School of Forestry

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, it was on the Luckiamute but it was down toward. . . It was on the old road towards Buena Vista, down in that area. Not on [Highway] 99, it was farther east on the Luckiamute.
entries.chapter_ref: 9. The Rawies and the OSC School of Forestry

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: On the old Independence Road?
entries.chapter_ref: 9. The Rawies and the OSC School of Forestry

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Uh huh.
entries.chapter_ref: 9. The Rawies and the OSC School of Forestry

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was the swimming hole pretty much on the highway there?
entries.chapter_ref: 9. The Rawies and the OSC School of Forestry

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, we had to walk through a field to get to it.
entries.chapter_ref: 9. The Rawies and the OSC School of Forestry

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And that is where the baptism was?
entries.chapter_ref: 9. The Rawies and the OSC School of Forestry

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That was where, as I recall. . . it was in that area.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So if you wanted to go anyplace with water from Wells, you had to drive someplace?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: We had to go quite a long.. . There wasn't any other creek or anything big enough to go swimming in.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now, was Bowers Slough...?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: But that was a slough. It wasn't a creek and it dried up in the summer time when a fella wanted to go swimming.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: 10. The Rawie Family Dairy

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Would there be things at the slough that kids would go through, like frogs or would ducks land there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't remember. I never did. As I say, the kids.. . When school was out for instance, we had chores to do in the evenings and in the summer time the kids all worked. I mean. . . I don't remember ever lacking something to do. You hear kids now, "1 don't have anything to do." There was always something to do.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Would you resent that or was that just the way that it was?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, that was just the way it was. My kids were brought up the same was when we came out here to the farm.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now, where you are living now, you used to farm in this area?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh yeah, we had a grade A dairy here and I milked cows here until 1962 I guess.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now the Wieses, were they next door to you?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: They lived up the road, up here on what is Walnut now. You've probably talked to Edna Wiese haven't you?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah, a few times.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, uh huh.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So, you had a daiiy farm.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. right here? So how many acres did you have? We had a 175 acres here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Huh. What do you think about all of these houses here now?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, it is different.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [Laughter]

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It is different

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So your boys were raised on a dairy farm?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh yeah, so when school was out at night, I never heard my kids at a lack of something to do. On Saturdays there were chores that had to be done. I always said that they would be good business people because they couldn't play until certain things were done so they would inveigle their city friends to come out and help them hail manure.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Kind of like Tom Sawyer.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: . . so that they could play then. They would bribe the city kids into letting them drive the tractor for a little while.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Would they play down here in Dixon Creek?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, Dixon Creek ran right down here behind us. They'd go down here and catch fish. Ralph and I would drive a hundred miles on the opening of fishing season to go fishing and we wouldn't catch anything and the two boys would stay home with their grandmother and go down here and they'd have a batch of trout for us when we got home. We caught a lot of fish out of our creek.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Is there still fish there now?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What happened?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't know. There is not much water in it anymore even.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What do you think happened to the water?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, I don't know. We had water rights off of the creek. There used to be a dam in it when we first came down here. We could have irrigated off of it but there wasn't too much water in it. Let's see, this street, Elmwood wasn't in here at that time We had 40 acres on that side of Dixon Creek and the rest was on this side. We went clear through to 10th Street which is Highland Way and then in an L shape up on the hill to where the Lutheran cemetery is.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Uh huk

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: 13th street would be where the L goes out. We sold this on this side first and then we started selling the other way down on Highland Way and we didn't sell it

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: all at one time until that got built up. We never developed it ourselves we'd sell it to a...

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: to a developer?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: a developer. Then when that was used up we'd sell another piece of it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you make more off of selling land or selling milk?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [Laughter] Much more off of seffing the land but we made it pay as a dairy farm too. My husband worked in town all of these years. He was service manager at the Ford Garage, so I did the milking. The boys did the feeding and stuff in the evening and Ralph did the feeding stuff in the morning and we would always get up at 4:30 a.m. and get the milking done and we'd be in the house by 7:00 a.m. so he could get showered and shaved and dressed up to get to town to work. Before we went to the milking parlor and the stainless steel tank where they come and pick the milk up, he hauled the milk to town in the Wilson Motor's truck as he'd go to work. He'd take the ten gallon cans of milk to the...

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, uh huh. Would Wilson Motors get upset about that?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: He was the seivice manager he...

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: He could do most anything he wanted.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Uh huh.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: As I say, it was quite an [inaudible]. It was a good life. It was a hard life. We'd change.. . the last time we changed. . . In the summer time we'd change the irrigation at 11:00 p.m. at night and we'd set a flashlight, lantern type flashlight, at the end where we wanted to take the pipe to. We had to change it all by hand. 600 feet of it. Sometimes in the morning it wasn't the straightest line in the world but we would get it across. In the mornings while I was milking, Ralph would go and change that pipe so it would run for another setting.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: It sounds like he was lucky that he married a tomboy.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh yeah, it was a family project.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you think that that was good for a family?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, it was wonderful! We worked together. We played together. When the kids were little I'd take them to the field with me and I'd drive the tractor to farm for

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: the day and I'd take the kids with me and take their little dump trucks and stuff and put them at the end of the furrow. I'd see them every time I came back. They'd just haul dirt and have a ball playing in the dirt all day with dump trucks and loaders. . . You know bow kids play with toys. It was a good life.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: 11. The Wells School

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: We were talldng about school before we started recording this. When you were growing up, your mother was involved with the school?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: She was chairman of the school board.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: For the Wells school?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Wells school.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was the Gingle's school still in existence then?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't think so. I never knew or saw a Gingle's school.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Eve,ybody came into Wells school?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Everybody came into Wells school.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What was the school like?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It was a two room school and it had a big stove in the room and then it had sort of a big metal shield around it, a reflector type, so kids couldn't get to close to it, you know. It set out quite a ways around the outside of the stove so no kids would get burned.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Would all of the grades be in the same room?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, there was two rooms. 1-4 and 4-8. .. . outside toilets, a play shed, and a shed where if any of the kids rode horses, they could tie their horses up and feed them.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was the school right in town there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, it was right.. . It would be the equivalent of probably two blocks from Grandpa's store. I always said that Grandpa gave away more stuff that he ever sold in the line of cookies or candy or else the kids just helped themselves. When school was out, the kids .. . and in the center of the floor he had a rack that had cookie jars in it with the metal lid that fit up, you know. They just automatically got themselves a cookie. I mean, they weren't stealing! That was just the way

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: that it was done.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Would they take four or five or just... ?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, I imagine that some of them did.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And your grandfather, that was fine with him?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, if they abused that fact, I can remember Grandpa saying, "We've had about enough," or something of the sort. But, one or two cookies was just alright. As I say, he gave away more stuff than he sold sometimes but, invariable, on Halloween they always put his buggy on top of the outhouse at the depot across the street. And he had to pay the same kids that put it up there to get it down the next day. [Laughter]

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So it was almost like a tradition? Ah ha. Would that get him upset?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh no, he just took to for granted.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Here's Halloween and my buggy is going to be on top of the outhouse?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Because at the deport, you know they had an outhouse and his buggy.. . I wouldn't say that. . . Yeah, I can remember that every year... I don't know how long that went on but I know for quite awhile. Of course, he had one of the first Model T Fords. I wish that I still had it. That would be really an antique.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah, the other schools in the district, say the kids that went to Tampico or Soap Creek or Mountain View or Berry Creelç was there any kind of competition? ... baseball or... ?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, there wasn't anything like that.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Scholastic competition?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: There was a spelling bee I guess but that was just amongst our kids. I don't remember of any outside activity, of any competitiveness between schools.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Or even visiting? . . . school plays or... ?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Uh huh. So it was all. . . Each one was kind of isolated? Each Community... ?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, Wells certainly was. We had one program a year and that was a Christmas program when the whole community came. It was a big deal. It had a big Christmas tree. When we were talking about Jakie Rohner [Jacob Rohner. See Monograph # 6].. . I remember that one year the Rohners didn't make it to the Christmas program because one of the girls ran her finger, making sausage you

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: know, through the grinder. I can't think which one of the girls it was. But anyway, somebody at the Rohner family cut their finger off with a food grinder and they didn't make it to the Christmas program. I haven't thought about that for a long time either.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now, the Rohners were Swiss...

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: . . and they were Catholics.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, Catholics. Was that something that they were know for?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh yeah, they went to Corvallis to church very religiously.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did other people think that that was odd?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, nobody.. . yes, not the religion, the Rohners were a little different. Now, don't misunderstand me, they didn't dress quite the same and they had home haircuts, well I had a home haircut too, but they were a little different. Wonderful people. Good as gold. Their dress or whatnot. . . They were just German or Swiss. . . and Mrs. Rohner, I don't think spoke much English.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Were there other members of the community that were from Europe or that had...

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, they were the only ones that I recall. They were a very strict family I think. Mr. Rohner, Big Jake, had a brother here in Corvallis that was a veterinarian for years, Doc Rohner. There were two girls, Selma and Nellie, that were about my age I think. Jake was a little older and then a lot of young ones, Elmer and Eddie. . . I can't think who all of them are.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Buddy?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [Inaudible] But as I say, they were quite strict. Even their dress sometimes was. I would call it old fashioned maybe. I'm not saying anything against them. They were lovely people but there was a difference in their family life I mean in their... kind of a cultural difference? Yes, that is right!

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: They had a lot of heritage from Europe.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That's right.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: The rest of the community, it sounds like, were pioneer stock

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: .from pioneer stock.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: . .   second and third generation.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, but the last couple of years.. . We have a picnic out at Helmick park for the people from the Camp Adair area and the Suver area.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, so Wells does get back together?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh yeah, and this summer Jakie, he was Jakie because his dad was Jake, and all through school Jake was Jakie and he is still Jakie to me, he came out to the picnic last year and I was so happy to see him. He has the most beautiful brown eyes. I mean I still. . . I remember that. He was so happy. I see him quite often around town or I used to I don't go downtown as much anymore. But I saw Robert McClain and oh, there are just an awful lot of people. The Barzees were all there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That is interesting that that community stayed together even though the war disrupted it.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Uh huh. It's our, Robert McClain's wife, what is her name?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yvonne [(brown) McClainJ.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Evonne. She sends out notices eveiy year. She is kind of the instigator of keeping it going. It is real fun to go back and we have a potluck dinner and there are a lot of people there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How did you pick Helmick park? Why didn't you go to Sulphur Springs?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well because Sulphur Springs. . . there isn't much out there. There are no tables or anything else. There hasn't been for a long time anyway. I haven't been to Sulphur Springs for a long time myself. Helmick park, primarily this was from... Evonne was from the Suver community which was just north of Wells about five miles on the railroad track to Suver, so as I say, she's the one that has kept it going but it is. . . the picnic is for the old timers from the Camp Adair area and the Suver area.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now this year will be the fiftieth anniversaiy of Camp Adair. Are you planning anything special for that?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I hadn't. . . nothing has been said that I've heard about that.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Hospital Hill is near the Ed Blake place, the school [OS U] owns that now and there is some talk of developing some sort of an interpretive display...

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: What school?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oregon State.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: .   . some kind of an interpretive display about Camp Adair. Fifty years coming up and it was an important event in the community's life and of course the school... We've got Dunn Forest that was all inherited from that era. What kind of theme in an interpretive display could be used to represent the Wells community or Welisdale? What kind of things would be good representations of that community?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, I would think the Carters were the mainstay of the Wells community. If I could get those pictures like of the store and of the postoffice, was all one, that I took out to the Benton County historical place. They could be used I would think.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And so the school would. .. because you're done with these other pictures... ?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: picture of the school and a picture of the store and I think that there was one of the depot. And they were pictures about [inaudible] . . . the same idea.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So you think that photographs of the old community would be good... ?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, that would be the type of thing. I have some old.. . see I've got an old... maybe you ought to turn that thing off.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: 12. Hamen Lewis

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Let's see, we are back in town and talking about the postoffice. One person that I'd like to go back to was Hamen Lewis, a lot of people mentioned Hamen Lewis. When you were kids you were warned not to go near him. What was the reason for that?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, we should be .. . not let him entice us into his house of something of that sort. He was kind of a character but as I. . . a rather interesting thing, when we bought this place it was a part of the original Hamen C. Lewis Donation Land Claim.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you know that when you bought it?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, not until after we bought it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And so you can remember the man that had this Donation Land Claim?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What was the reason that you weren't supposed to go into his house, was he...?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: He had a tendency to want to handle little girls.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, and so they warned you about that?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, and so we just weren't ever. . . He would sit on the porch and he'd always want you to come and sit on his lap or something of the sort. And I'm not saying that he ever did, but in those days we were warned, as people are today, to just don't do things like that.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: A lot of people I talk to say that back in the old days people were nicer, better, but it sounds like really people were kind of the same in certain ways.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: In some ways, yeah. He was a loner. I don't remember that he... I know that he had two grown sons Ralph and somebody else. They would be my aunt's age. I got.. . you know they used to send cards with pictures on them that were postcards, like you'd put a penny stamp on them, but they had pictures. . . . I got some in there from Lewis, Ralph Lewis, to my aunt because they were about the same age and grew up in the town of Wells. But as I say, it was always interesting, I thought, that when we bought this place that it was part of the Hamen Lewis DLC.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now, other than being warned not to go too close, what would he do for a living?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Mr. Lewis? I don't know! He never did anything all the years that I knew him.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Just hung out at the store?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Uh huh, but he must have some money from someplace. It was a big old house that he lived in. Filthy dirty inside. When he would get sick, my grandmother would go down once in awhile and fix him something to eat. He was just kind of weirdly.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What would he talk about?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't remember he'd sit and cross his legs and this foot. Isn't this funny but I can remember that foot [inaudible] .. . dirty. His clothes got pretty dirty.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Everybody mentions him. They say it wasn't Herman it was Hamen and...

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It was Hamen, Hamen C. Lewis.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And he made an impression on everybody?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, I'm sure he did. He did on me. I mean, I was always told. . . and when I

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: got a little older I worked behind the counter and that's where the till was and I was always told never, when Hamen was in the store, should I get cornered behind the counter. That was just something that we didn't do.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now, do you know of any case of him actually doing something?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I don't. But apparently someplace along the line there must have been something done. That was why it was impressed on all of the younger girls especially and even the boys weren't supposed to go in his house. I can remember that too.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So he's done something... ?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Someplace along the line there was a reason for it because people didn't ordinarily pick up on that sort or thing. It wasn't a story that was told without some ground. It wasn't malicious gossip in those days. There was a reason for it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And so the kids... Now, did people... Other than keeping their kids away from him, would people ostracize him or treat him different?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, he wasn't social at all. He wasn't social. He wore an old hat. He was a big man, a real big man. And even Mother Rawie, I mean she didn't. . . Grandma Carter, that's who it was, I was thinking about Mother Rawie, Mother Rawie was on the other side of the story. I shouldn't get into that. She was "Mrs. 5x5," Ralph's mother was. She resembled my grandmother quite a bit, is why I said that. But Grandma Rawie never took any chances with him. It was just something that people didn't do.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: They just gave him his space? Were they afraid of him or...?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, I don't think that he was malicious. I mean, in that sort of a way, he had a thing for young girls. That was the warning that we had.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That is something though that when you were growing up you knew people that had actually crossed the Oregon Trail and had settled on Donation Land Claims. Did people have any of the sense of that? Did they give special credit to their ancestors or to local people that had crossed the Oregon Trail?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, I think that in older days everybody was brought up to respect their elders a lot more than they do now.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was that seen as a special type of event though, that maybe set certain elders away from

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: other elders?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't know. I don't know.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you ever hear of the Applegate Trail when you were growing up?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, and I didn't . . . I learned a lot more about history since I have gotten older but I

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: 13. Grandma Carter

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: We were just talking about histoiy. I was wonderin& you say as you got older you got more interested in history, what do you think history is good for?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, I don't know quite how to answer that other than I think that the reason that I have become more interested in.. . When you are a kid you're not interested in it, there are other things. Then, as you get older and you have kids of your own and you start to tell them something and you have to stop and think all of a sudden; how did that happen or when did that happen? I think the older I get the more interested I am getting.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: You've been real helpful with this project and with pictures and eveiythin    what is the value you see in helping projects out like this?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, I think that other people are interested and I think that. . . I am proud of my heritage and I'm proud of the country that I live in and I'm proud of the state of Oregon and whatnot and I'd just like to pass it on to people.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So you know that people are interested and you'd like to share it?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, and as I say, I am proud of what my family did to help settle Oregon. I'm proud to be an Oregonian, part of the community, and I think it's just nice to pass it on for other people to know about.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So, part of it is providing entertainment for other people and part of it's preselving our heritage?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That's right. Uh huh.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Other than Hamen Lewis, where you aware of any other people who came across the Oregon Trail?.. . and Grandma Carter of course.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, of course. Well, basically not really. When I lived out there all of the

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: people up there were related basically. Not really but, Grandma Carter... Everybody knew Grandma Carter she was the...

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: was the focal point of the community?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well yeah, because of her age. She lived so long. Now she really wasn't part of the Wells community because she lived farther away up closer to Palestine. She was known all over the state of Oregon because of her age.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And it was stiictly because of her age?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So she was like one of the oldest people in the state?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, and the older she got the more people that came from all over the country to interview her and to talk. She loved every minute of it!

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, she liked the attention?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh yes!

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Would people in the community see her about other things? Would they go visit her just to.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: A lot of people went to visit her just because she was a novelty, I mean, because of her age she was different. She had seen a lot. People loved to talk to her and she loved to visit.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was she kind of a character or more matronly or something?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: She was a lady. She had a wonderful memory and she could tell.. . As I say, when I was a kid and went to see her, I took her for granted. She was just Grandma Carter!

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you like having a famous grandmother?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I didn't realize that she was famous when I was a kid. The older I got. . . What's the old saying? . . . I said it about my mother. . . the older I got the smarter my mother got. I mean, it was me that got smarter but that was the same way with Grandma Carter, the older I got the more I realized what a remarkable person she was, but when you are around someone like that, you take them for granted. She was your grandma and...

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What do you think when you see anicles about her in the paper?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, I was thrilled to death. That's what I was hunting for, a scrapbook that has

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: all of these articles about her, about a lot of things. It's in my dad's trunk in there but I just couldn't find it in a huriy. I think now why I'm getting more interested. . . my oldest granddaughter graduates from Crescent Valley High school this year and is going on to college . . . she's going on up to Missoula, Montana [University of Montana at Missoula] if fact, she and her dad are up there now. . . and she is going to major in history. She loves it! Half of her projects in High schools have been writing on family stuff. on her family histoiy? And she is' only in High school? Uh huh, and she just loves it. Now she has a computer of her own and she is putting all of her stuff on her computer.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Good for her. Why is she not going to Oregon State?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, she wanted to go away to school and that is fine. I think that that is good for her and she's a student. Her folks don't have any problems about her going away to school. She's a good student. She could be a lot better student if she she loves to read but she doesn't always read .. . she likes to read novels and stuff like that as well as other things. You could never punish Tonya5 [Tonya Michelle Rawie] by sending her to her room because on her way she'd grab a book and she'd stay there all day!

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [Laughter]

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: She was tickled to death.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: It sounds like you have a family historian that you are raising.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, she's really interested. In fact, after I got this letter from this lady that I told you about, you know, the one that called and wanted to know if I was the one that. . . each one of my sons had gotten the same letter. She had gone through the phone directory apparently, and had written to all of the Rawies. But immediately, Tonya had gone out to the cemetery and had taken pictures of all of the tombstones with the Carter names on them and sent them to her.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: A/i, good

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That's a picture of us [Pointing to a family photograph]. They wanted their picture taken with their grandmother so we had our picture taken.

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: 5 Tonya's sister is Traci Melinda Rawie.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Is she the one to the left?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: caption
entries.text: Wells Public School, c.1910.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: 14. Local Schools and Wildflowers

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Uh huh, you talked about schools and then didn't relate to them much but you knew their names. Did you ever hear the Mountain View school called Drum school?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It has always been the Mountain View school as long as I can remember. But as I say, I never even. . . I guess you'd call me naive as a kid. . . I never even knew about Mountain View school when I lived out of... [Wells].

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Is that right?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: You'd never heard of it?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I mean...

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about Beriy Creek school?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I didn't. I don't remember ever hearing anything about Berry Creek school or I didn't care anything about it if I did when I was going to school, when I lived out there. Suver or Tampico... well Tampico wouldn't have a school.. . Soap Creek? [School] No, there was a school at Tampico.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, that's right.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't remember the Soap Creek school up there until it was made into a museum type thing. It was kind of a funny little old building up there but I don't remember it being a school. Tampico, I remember it was there on the corner where about three roads come together there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you remember any stories about Tampico?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, but there seems to be. . . I don't even know what I heard. . . I won't even say it because. . . but it was kind of a ruff and tumble sort of place. I don't know. Was there a saloon there or something in the area?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: There was the. . . Arcade Saloon (Tampico) was there. You always hear people remember it as a rowdy place but nobody can remember exactly why.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: As I say, and this would just be heresay of what I've heard because I don't know anything about it.. . I remember the old school sitting there on the triangle and they used to have hay in it after it quit being used as a school. I don't remember anything about.. . What was the other one?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Beny Creek [School]

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I don't remember Berry Creek.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: This is an odd question, do you remember any jackrabbits?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: We had a few jackrabbits.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: You did?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [Inaudible] bunny rabbits.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Were they bunny rabbits or jackrabbits?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Jackrabbits are those big, long eared ones aren't they?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I don't remember any of those. We had the little ones that came in and ate the garden but not a jackrabbit per Se. . . . like they have over in eastern Oregon.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now on Soap Creek, you mentioned going to Sulphur Springs, the Luckia,nute, but Soap Creek went up through that area north of you, how come you never went there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: There was no Soap Creek up there close to Wells.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Didn't it go north up by Suver up there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I can't think of it. There would be. . . Maybe there was a little creek that ran up through there but I don't remember that it was called Soap Creek.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now, Calloway Creek, that came in the Bowers Slough doesn't it?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, so that is why you wouldn't go to...?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I don't. . . and I never. . . This was always the Soap Creek area out there were Sulphur Springs is, to me, that's Soap Creek. I don't remember it being any other place but up there. I lived out there for an awful lot of years.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So as it went east of Coffin Butte, you don't have any idea where it went?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't know what happened to it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So, you think more of the valley then?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, uh huh.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: On Hospital Hill, do you know where that is at?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, that's the hill in back of the Ed Blake place and it became Hospital Hill because of Camp Adair, so that wasn't the old name for it. It's where the reservoir for the town of

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Adair Village.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I know where Ed Blake lives.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: But you don't remember the hill there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I don't remember. I know where they live out there. I got a picture down in the basement of their house. It was just a print.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: An old picture of their place?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, not of their place, but it was a picture out of their house when they moved to Corvallis. The Blakes where real good friends of my mothers and they all belonged to the Mountain View Grange. Ed and Lottie Blake were.. . She was a school teacher.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Where did she teach school at?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't know, but I think that my dad went to school to her. Not very long because he never went past the fifth grade. Of course he couldn't walk to suit the teacher and I guess his daughter kind of got a little bit of his. . . I went to school, I don't mean that, but I am pretty set in my ways. I don't do something just because it is being done. I mean, [Laughter]

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So, your dad didn't see eye to eye with the teacher in the fifth grade and called it quits?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: And so he just walked out and he never went back.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now, fake Rohner didn't finish much beyond that but he said that in those days a farmer didn't need to know much except how to farm.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, that is what I remember. In fact, my oldest boy, David, who is 52 now, walked home from school when he was in second grade and when he left he told the teacher that there was just too much to do on the farm and he was going home. She called me up and said that, "David is on his way home and he says that there is just too much to do on the farm and that school is a waste of time." I said, "Don't worry, he'll be back tomorrow." She said, "Well I figured that." [Laughter] He walked from where Franklin school is down there by Fred Meyer's, the old Franklin school by Fred Meyer's, and he walked home packing all of his books. When he got home I said, "What are you doing home?" He said, "I came home because there is too much work to do out here to spend time in school." I said, "Okay, but you are going back to school tomorrow." "Yup." I

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: never made an issue of it. That was all that was said.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So he is pretty independent?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh yeah, and he is still independent.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now you said that you were kind of the same way but you made it through High schooL

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, I went through High school and I went to Business College. I'm not a social climber. . . you take me for what I am or you leave me alone. That was the way that my dad was and that's the way David is. He has lots of friends and has done very well but he is his own person.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Uh huh. This is backing up a little bit, but when we were talking about the wildlife, I forgot to ask about wildflowers on the fann.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, buttercups and, well I called them flags, wild iris, and that sort of stuff, and then you went up on Coffin Butte. . . We always had to go up there in the spring time. We could find ladyslippers...

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, so you went up to Coffin Butte for the ladyslippers?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Would all the kids do it or would the adults do it?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I would go because my aunt and uncle lived up there on the side of the Butte so I could walk over there and cross old [Hwy] 99 and then I could walk the sheep trail over and come into my aunt and uncle's house from the back side of it. It would be on the east side of Coffins Butte where they've dug it all out now. I'll never forget one time when I was a little kid and I walked up there and when I came home I took home a little lamb. Mother said, "Where did you get that little lamb!" I said, "Well mother, it was lost. It was up there asleep all by itself! Well, you know how a mother Eve will leave it's baby to sleep and it will go off to eat and I was sure that mother had gone off and left it and it was going to die and so I took it home. I marched right back with it. I had to go back all by myself and take it back up the side of the hill. [Laughter]

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How old were you then?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I must have been seven or eight years old.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Are you   ... You said ladyslippers and you were going to say birds.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: birdsbills and, we called them cat's ears. Have you seen those little gray

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: flowers that are fuzzy on the inside? Looked like little ears. Lamb tongues. There was one spot up there around the spring where we could find trilliums, a lily type of thing.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Where was the spring at?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: There was a spring up.. . Well, my aunt and uncle got their water from a spring on Coffins Butte.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now you say Coffins Butte, but I've heard other people say Coffin Butte.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, it's C-o-f-f-i-n but I guess I did put it in the plural but it is just Coffin Butte. I'm sure of it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, because there Lc a family named Coffin that married into the Beriy family and I am kind of curious if maybe they didn't name it after that family of something.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't know but it is Coffin Butte. If I slurred it into an "s" there, I didn't do it intentionally.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. Now up there on top of Coffin Butte, I've heard stories of an Indian buriaL Have you ever heard those stories?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It seems like as a kid, but I was never for sure whether it was or if it was just a tale that somebody tried to scare us kids with to try to keep us from. . . We always climbed the Butte in the spring. That was the thing to do. Like Ruth [Torgeson], this little gal that I told you lived over there, and some of us, we always climbed the Butte. That was a high...

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Just for the view?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, we'd get up there and look all around.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: 15. The Dust Storm of 1931

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Can you remember the snow storm of 1937?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I should because that was the year that I was married. No, I was married in '38. No, I don't remember a bad snow storm. We had a real bad dust storm. My aunt and uncle's [Eston and Anna (Torgeson) Carter] house burnt during the dust storm and we didn't even know it. That was...

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What can you remember about that dust storm?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, it was just a dust storm. It was just terrible! It was just something that we

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: just don't have in this country, but really they lived. . . We could see their house from our house but their house burned and we didn't even know it until they came and told us after it was all over with.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How long did it last?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, as a kid it just seems that it lasted for an awfully long time. It probably lasted two or three days.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, a long time.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, it wasn't just something that went through and...

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did people have any idea? Was there any stories about where it was coming from?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I just remember that awful dust storm when Mox's house burnt. As a kid, that is what I remember. I associated their house burning with the dust storm.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And that was right on the base of the Butte there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, well they were up kind of up . . . They weren't right down along the Highway. They were up the road that went to the Rohner's place and then you turned off of that through a gate and went up to their house.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Uh huh. Do you remember if the dust was any particular color or anything?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It was dust colored. [Laughter] And you couldn't breathe. I mean, it was Well, it was the only time that I have seen anything like it. As I see things in movies and whatnot now, I always think about it because it was bad.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Uh huh, was there any stories about where the dust came from?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I don't remember anything about that. Everybody was glad when it was gone but there wasn't much discussion of why or where or. . . as far as I was concerned.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did it leave any deposits around town?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: It just kind of blew through and blew clean?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Blew in and blew out. The houses were especially dusty inside, I mean. . . but there wasn't. . . I don't remember a lot of wind, a driving wind with it, but it had to come in on the wind but it wasn't a tornado type of a wind or something like that. The dust had to come in in the wind but it wasn't a violent wind storm as I recall.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: It is an interesting event. Can you remember any snow storms or ice storms in particular?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't remember anything.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about floods? Can you remember the flood in 1941?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, I can remember floods that we had here in town before the dams went in.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Wells wouldn't be effected by those?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, we never had any high water out there. Surface water over the roads but no. .   But see, there was no rivers out there to flood! We were too far away from the Luckiamute. The Luckiamute flooded, but that didn't effect us. There was a little creek that ran through, but it dried up in the summer time. I mean, there just wasn't any...

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How did people get their water was it all... ?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: They had wells, drilled wells. A lot of them had dug wells.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Would that be how the town got it's name? .. . Mill Creek, Fossil...

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't know. I don't know where Wells got it's name.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you remember any wind storms at all? Anything like the Columbus Day storm?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, the Columbus Day storm I remember well, but we were living here at the time. But that is the only thing like that and that was really something.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: 16. Poison Oak

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Of course, we've got a good history on that with newspapers and everything else. I've got two more questions here, actually I can think of a third one, and then before I get into them I'd like you to think of something that we haven't covered that you think. . . about your family or the Wells community or some of the events... We haven't talked to much about Holidays.    . . . something that maybe you've done or your family has obseived or something that occurred that we haven't touched on or brought up. Does anything come to mind immediately?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, the questions... One is do you remember any pine trees out there? Any trees at all?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, we had an oak grove on our farm which would probably be the equivalent of about an acre. It's still out there. I could never understand why the Camp didn't bulldoze it out but it didn't. There was maple trees around the school

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: house. Up on the Butte, that's what we called it, there used to be a few fir trees but no, there wasn't. . . As a forest goes, there wasn't anything like that. It was farm ground.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you remember any camas out there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Any what?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Camas. A blue plant with bulbs that the Indians used to eat. ... or wild onions or anything like that?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: It was all cultivated pretty much?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Uh huh.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: When Camp Adair came out there there were...?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: lots of poison oak when Camp Adair came.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was there poison oak before that?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh yes! And that's what all the soldier boys got, poison oak. It was terrible. And they sprayed, and they sprayed, and they sprayed for poison oak but it is all coming back. It was up around Rohner's place and whatnot out there. [Inaudible] still getting pretty bad poison oak.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Would you kids get poison oak?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Not from that, but they would get poison oak.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Is there more poison oak now than there used to be?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I don't think that there is anymore but my kids are both woodcutters. I mean, they love to go out and cut their own wood so they usually come home with a good batch of poison oak. [Laughter]

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Uh huh. The ridge where Peavy Arboretum was, that used to be called Tampico Ridge, Beals Hills was a pair of it, do you recall those names?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well of course I knew where the Beals lived. They lived right across the street from the Glenders. I don't know what's in there know. Does the college own it?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: All the Glenders side and the other side is private.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, okay.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you remember... Was that hill called Beals Hill?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, the Beals were down on the low side. I don't remember it called Beals Hill.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was it Glenders Hill?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Glenders. I would think of it as Glenders Hill. Whether that was what it was, but if I was referring to that hill I would call it Glenders Hill.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you do that when you were a kid? Would you say Glenders Hill or anything?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, when you would say Glenders Hill you would just say, "Over by Glenders." I don't remember it being called a hill, it was just [inaudible].

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: We were talking about poison oak and I was bringing that to mind and those hills in there, that Tampico Ridge is marked on maps as Poison Oak HilL

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh.   .   . Well where I was thinking about all of the poison oak, you know, where the Rohners lived and then coming south all along the Highway there where they have planted some new Christmas trees in there and there is an Arabian Horse place in there now along in there; that hill was just solid poison oak. That's where the boys went, the army boys went, out on bivouac and stuff, up in there. Oh, they got poison oak!

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How did you hear about all of that?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, after all, we had an army boy staying with us in town and you heard it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: It is called Poison Oak Hill now on the maps, do you think that it might have come from that era?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I think that's where it got the name Poison Oak Hill. Boy, those soldier boys were in bad shape!

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: 17. Local Black History

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now, when the army came in, you said that there were actually no minorities of any kind in the community; no chinese or blacks?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I don't remember anybody but we had everything after the Camp came in here to Corvallis.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was there any resistance to that?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No there wasn't any, I wouldn't say. I have always felt that Corvallis handled the situation real good.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: There was no racial problems?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I never heard of any.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Can you remember any black people that lived in Corvallis when you moved here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I think that there has always been one family as long as I can remember. . . one black family in here. Of course, there are lots now. And there was one Filipino that lived here who was a. . . a little fella who was sort of a janitor or caretaker for a lot of the businesses in town. There was never any racial things but we hear a lot about it now in recent years, but I don't remember as a kid growing up or after I was married and living here in town. I don't remember anything about there being racial tensions here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you remember the name of the black family that lived here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No. Of course when my kids where in school, there was always the Reynolds family, of course, but they are not from long way back but you know the Reynolds family were very athletic here [inaudible] . . . And they were of course in school with my kids but as far as my family and my association, there was never any difference in the people. I mean, they were different but I mean we didn't... They weren't differentiated by status or anything. I mean, they weren't looked down on or anything within our own family.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you remember a man named Bud Smith?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, Bud Smith I remember. Yeah, I remember him.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was that the black family you were referring to?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I think that was the family. Yeah, I couldn't think of that but when you said that, I can remember that now.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: The Smith family was pretty well accepted?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, they were just accepted.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: 18. The Good Life

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: The other question that I have is a lot of the Camp Adair has become the Wilson Game Farm. Do you remember anything about E.E. Wilson?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I know that it's E.E. Wilson Game Ranch but I don't know who E.E. Wilson is. I presumed that he had something to do with forestry or wildlife or something but I never thought much about it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So, that's just a name?

entries.speaker: caption
entries.text: Velma Carter and Bessie Price, walking to Wells school along the Red Electric railroad tracks, c.1921.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That's just a name.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now, there used to be a game bird ranch out there that the state operated. Was that...

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: There still is.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was that there when you were a kid?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, that only has come in there since the Camp was there. That land out there all belonged to Camp Adair and then the state took it over as a game reserve.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That's every question that I can think of. [Laughter] Can you think of anything else that we haven't touched on or that you'd be interested in getting recorded?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, I can't. I can't really think of anything. It was the only life I knew. I was a very. . . Well my husband always said that I had never been out of the state of Oregon until he married me, which was true. I just. . . We just worked and ate and slept I guess and enjoyed life.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: It sounds like it was a good life.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I was a good life! I think that's why when Ralph and I were married and we finally came back to the farm, that's the way our life was. It was a family project. We all worked and we ate and we . . . The more we worked, the more we could have to eat and the more we could have to do everything. The more profitable the farm was why.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now you have a granddaughter writing about it.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. [Laughter]

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I would sure like to thank you for your time doing this.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well I've enjoyed it. It may all sound a little silly and far fetched and whatnot but it's.. And I'm real proud of my heritage and the Carter... That area out . there was basically was Carter's.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: This is the kind of thing that is going to keep it alive.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, that is right. And I realize that.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: APPENDIX A

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: The following summary of the history of Wells, Oregon was written in longhand by Velma Rawie for Lorna Grabe of the Soap Creek Schoolhouse Foundation, c. 1985. A copy of the original is on file with the Cultural Resources Manager for OSU Research Forests. A note on the manuscript states that 'Wells was an early town located where the [E. E.] Wilson Game Farm is now."

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: Wells Station

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: Historical Notes by Velma Rawie

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: I am the great-granddaughter of Tolbert and Angelina Carter, the granddaughter of John A. and Mary C. Carter and the daughter of E.P. (Pearl) and Rose E. Carter. My name is Velma P. Rawie and I was born at Wells, Oregon. I was asked to write about my recollections of that town. My grandfather J.A. Carter was store owner and post master for forty-eight years. The store was the center of the community. A wood stove at the back of the store was surrounded by chairs, nail kegs and benches and many stories and discussion were held as the men of the community met to wait the mail trains. These was a minimum of four mail trains a day. If there was no passengers or freight, the trains merely slowed for the exchange of mail bags. The first passenger and mail trains were electric, sort of like the trolley cars. They ran between Portland and Corvallis. There was a substation at Wells. Later the trains were steam with a mail car, passenger cars and freight all in one train.

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: The freight and passengers depot was across the street and tracks from the street and post office and was called Wellsdale to keep it from being confused with Wells, Nevada. My father E. P. (Pearl) Carter was freight and passenger agent before he and my mother bought a farm nearby. There was a switching track so trains could pass on load and it was always a treat when a refrigerated car was parked on the siding. We were able to climb on top and open the ice compartments and get ice. This meant we might be able to have homemade ice cream.

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: As I think back, I'm sure granddad gave away or had taken, all of his profit. The kids all stopped by after school and all seemed to get a hand in the cookie container and bulk candy jars.

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: Across the tracks at the depot there was outside toilets----one side for men, the other for women. Every Halloween, Granddad's buggy wound up on top of the outhouse. He had to pay (Irma Price, the same kids that put it up there) to have it taken down. This was almost a ritual every year and the kids weren't considered delinquent either.

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: There was also a community Church where Sunday school was held every Sunday and visiting preachers held church nearly every Sunday. The Artisan Hall was the social Center. Dances and parties, quilting bees, elections, the Christmas program and of

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: course lodge meeting were held here. There was a large grain elevator and warehouse where farmers brought their grain. My father worked at the warehouse during harvest after he moved to the farm.

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: The school house was a two room school. Four grades in each room. It was District #1 in Benton County. It was located about where the present game farm managers home is.

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: We closed the store and post office in January 1936 because of Grandpa's ill health. My great-grandmother died in February 1936, grandpa in July of 1936, Grandma in June of 1937 and my father December, 1937.

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: My husband Ralph and I moved from Corvallis to Wells to help mother with the farm after dad passed away and our two sons David and Melvin were born in 1939 and 1941 while we lived at Wells.

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: With the bombing of Pearl Harbor on December 7, 1941 there was much confusion in the area about condemnation of land for a military base---soon and the old timers were removed from their land and homes. This we included my family and so came an end to Wells, Oregon. Early in 1942 the first flag was raised over Camp Adair.
